key_idea: Cut the manifold along one-sided-minimizing stable minimal hypersurfaces until you reach a Frankel-type core, attach cylindrical ends, and use min-max on the non-compact result. The cylindrical ends force the widths to grow linearly, with each gap at least the boundary area, while each width must be a multiple of the area of a single interior minimal hypersurface, and an equidistribution argument shows these two facts are incompatible.
reason: The core idea is striking and explains the result well. Gluing on cylindrical ends turns the stable boundary into a linear 'cylindrical Weyl law', and comparing that with the Frankel-type rigidity in the core gives a clear reason why finitely many minimal hypersurfaces is impossible. The surrounding work is heavy, though: building the non-smooth cylindrical metric, confining the min-max limits, the cutting lemmas with several cases, and a fiddly Weyl-equidistribution arithmetic lemma all add bookkeeping that keeps this short of a book proof.
recognized: Antoine Song, 'Existence of infinitely many minimal hypersurfaces in closed manifolds' (proof of Yau's conjecture)
